history:
The Autódromo José Carlos Pace, more commonly known as Interlagos, has been the heart of Brazilian motorsport since its opening in 1940. Situated in São Paulo, it was named in honor of the Brazilian Formula One driver who tragically died in a plane crash in 1977. While Interlagos is most famous for hosting the Brazilian Grand Prix, it has also hosted various other racing series, including motorcycle racing events on the specifically designed Moto Circuit layout. The Moto Circuit, though less celebrated than the full Grand Prix layout, provides a challenging and exciting experience for two-wheeled competition. It retains much of the character of the full circuit, providing a fitting test for the world's best motorcycle racers.

Although Formula 1 has been the mainstay of Interlagos' racing calendar, the Moto Circuit layout has hosted a number of important national motorcycle races, including rounds of the Brazilian Superbike Championship. It offers a unique challenge for riders, combining fast flowing corners with technical sections that demand precision and control. The Moto Circuit's relatively shorter length creates a more intense and compact racing experience for both competitors and spectators.
atmosphere: Standing at the Senna S during a Brazilian Superbike race on the Moto Circuit layout is an experience unlike any other. The roar of the engines echoes through the grandstands, a symphony of high-revving inline-fours and thunderous V-twins. The vibrant colors of the Brazilian flag are everywhere, draped over the barriers and painted on faces. The air crackles with excitement as riders jostle for position, their leathers brushing against each other as they navigate the tight corners. The smell of burning rubber and high-octane fuel hangs heavy in the air, a visceral reminder of the raw power and adrenaline on display. The passionate Brazilian fans erupt in cheers with every overtake, creating an electrifying atmosphere that makes you feel like you're part of the action.
trackCharacter: The Moto Circuit at Interlagos, with its 4.1km length and 14 turns, presents a unique blend of speed and technicality. Unlike the full Grand Prix layout, it emphasizes a more compact and flowing rhythm, requiring riders to maintain momentum through a series of linked corners. The elevation changes, a hallmark of Interlagos, are still present, adding another layer of complexity. The track rewards riders who are smooth and precise, able to carry maximum corner speed while managing the bumps and undulations. It’s a circuit that demands respect and rewards bravery, offering a thrilling challenge for both seasoned professionals and amateur racers alike. The shortened layout also brings the spectators closer to the action, creating a more intense and intimate racing experience.

famousCorners.name: Senna S
famousCorners.description: A fast, flowing chicane at the start of the lap. The first two corners are taken in quick succession, usually in 2nd or 3rd gear depending on setup.
famousCorners.challenge: Requires a precise entry and exit to maintain momentum for the climb up the hill.

famousCorners.name: Curva do Sol
famousCorners.description: A long, sweeping right-hander that leads onto the back straight. One of the fastest corners on the Moto Circuit.
famousCorners.challenge: Demands a high level of commitment and bravery, as riders must carry maximum speed through the corner to set up an overtaking opportunity on the following straight.

famousCorners.name: Descida do Lago
famousCorners.description: A downhill section with a series of quick changes in direction. Requires the rider to quickly shift their weight to maintain grip and stability.
famousCorners.challenge: Keeping the bike settled over the bumps and staying on the racing line. It's easy to run wide here.

famousCorners.name: Junção
famousCorners.description: A slow, tight left-hander that connects the back straight to the final sector.
famousCorners.challenge: A critical corner for setting up the final few turns. Braking is crucial, but so is maintaining corner speed for the run to the finish line.

famousCorners.name: Curva do Café
famousCorners.description: A slow, hairpin corner that leads onto the main straight. One of the best overtaking opportunities on the Moto Circuit.
famousCorners.challenge: Getting the braking point right and making a clean exit to maximize acceleration onto the main straight.

overtakingSpots: End of the back straight after Curva do Sol
historySnippets: The track was originally much longer, over 8km in its early years.
José Carlos Pace, the track's namesake, won the Brazilian Grand Prix here in 1975.
The Moto Circuit configuration utilizes portions of the full Grand Prix circuit.
Interlagos is known for its undulating layout and challenging corners.
Many famous drivers and riders consider Interlagos to be one of their favorite circuits.
weatherNotes: São Paulo's weather is notoriously unpredictable, and Interlagos is no exception. Rain is a common occurrence, often turning races into treacherous affairs. The track's undulating surface and painted run-off areas can become extremely slippery in wet conditions. Even when it's dry, the high altitude can affect engine performance, requiring careful setup adjustments. Humidity is also a factor, impacting rider stamina and concentration.
drivingAdvice: On the Moto Circuit layout, maintaining momentum is key. The flowing nature of the track rewards riders who are smooth and precise with their inputs. The Senna S requires a perfect line to set up the rest of the lap. Be patient and don't overdrive the corners, especially in the Descida do Lago, where it's easy to lose time. The final sector is crucial, so make sure to get a good run out of the Junção to set up a pass into Curva do Café. Be prepared for sudden changes in grip, especially if the weather is unpredictable.
famousRaces: 1991 Brazilian Grand Prix: Ayrton Senna's legendary victory with a failing gearbox.
2003 Brazilian Grand Prix: Giancarlo Fisichella's surprise win in a rain-soaked race.
2008 Brazilian Grand Prix: Felipe Massa wins, but Lewis Hamilton claims his first F1 title in dramatic fashion on the last lap.
localCulture: São Paulo is a vibrant metropolis, a melting pot of cultures and cuisines. The local 'churrascarias' offer a delicious taste of Brazilian barbecue, while the 'feijoada' is a must-try traditional stew. The passion for motorsport runs deep in the Brazilian culture, and the fans at Interlagos are some of the most enthusiastic and knowledgeable in the world. The paddock is always buzzing with activity, a mix of international teams and local talent, all united by their love of racing.
